text.text: Your portfolio in one place. Check Rent payments due, Leases ending soon, Maintenance requests scheduled this week, and which Units are vacant. Operational tracking only; keep signed leases and notices in your document system.
Rent collection is the heartbeat of the business. The same steps every month, done on the same days, keep late rent rare and fair.
A rent row exists for every active lease for the coming cycle
Reminder sent three days before the due date with how to pay
Any payment plans from last month checked
On and after the due date
Record each payment as it arrives:
Partial payments: record what arrived and set
When the grace period in the lease ends, mark unpaid rows
the lease allows, and send a friendly late notice.
Call every late tenant within two days. Most late rent is a timing problem, not a refusal.

cells.text: Second call; offer a written payment plan
Formal notice to pay or quit, only as your state's process requires

text.text: Never lock out a tenant, remove belongings or cut utilities. Follow the legal process only.

Quentin's rent is two days late and he has given notice. The manager calls, learns his paycheck lands Friday, notes a promise to pay and checks again Monday.

Start with a question, not a demand: "Your rent hasn't arrived yet. Is everything all right?" Write down what they promise and when, then follow up on that exact day. Being consistent matters more than being strict; tenants talk to each other, and a landlord who treats everyone the same gets fewer disputes.
Offer at least one electronic method and record which one each tenant uses. Cash payments always get a written receipt.
Every vacant day costs rent. A tight turnover gets the unit rented within two to three weeks of move-out.
on the lease and confirm the move-out date in writing.
. Start marketing with photos taken before the tenant leaves, with permission.
Schedule a pre-move-out walk-through so the tenant can fix small things and get more of the deposit back.
Move-out inspection with photos, compared with the move-in report
Forwarding address collected for the deposit
Clean, paint, repairs, carpet or floor work, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors tested.
Add each job as a maintenance request so cost and vendor are tracked.
Aim for a finished unit within seven days.
Return the deposit with an itemized list of deductions within the time your state requires. Deductions are for damage beyond normal wear, with photos and receipts. Record the return on the old lease.
Photos of every room in daylight, plus the outside and parking.
A clear rent, deposit, pet policy and move-in date in every ad.
Answer every inquiry the same day and offer two showing times.
Price from comparable rentals nearby; a unit still empty after two weeks of showings is usually priced too high.
Screen every applicant the same way with written criteria.
Sign the lease, collect the deposit and first month, and do a move-in inspection with photos.
Millrace downstairs is in turnover with a paint touch-up scheduled. Showings start this weekend so a new lease can begin the week the paint dries.

Set a standard budget per unit size so the team does not have to ask for approval on every small job. Anything above it waits for the owner's yes. Compare the real cost on the maintenance requests with the budget after every turn.
Fast, fair repairs keep good tenants. Triage tells you what to do now, what this week, and what can wait.

text.text: Tell tenants to call 911 or the gas company first for gas smells and fires.
Log it with unit, priority, trade and a clear title.

Twice a year: furnace and air conditioning service, smoke and CO detector tests, gutter cleaning, water heater check. Log each as a routine request so the history is kept per unit.

The sparking outlet at Alderwood was logged as an emergency; the electrician was there the same day. The jammed disposal was caused by a utensil, so it is marked to charge to the tenant with the vendor's note.

Tell the tenant three things: when the vendor is coming, roughly how long it will take, and who to call if nobody shows. Follow up the day after to confirm it is fixed. Requests that sit without an update are the biggest source of tenant complaints, even when the repair itself is quick.
Keep two vendors per trade with their insurance on file, and note response times. Use the faster one for emergencies.
Keeping a good tenant is almost always cheaper than finding a new one. Start renewals early and price them fairly.
Filter leases ending in the next 90 days.
Look at the tenant's payment history and any maintenance issues.
Check market rent for similar units nearby.
Decide the offer: renew at the same rent, a modest increase, or not renew (follow your local law on notice and reasons).
Send it in writing with the new rent in
, the term and a reply-by date.
Mention any upgrades you will make on renewal; small improvements help good tenants stay.
Signed renewal stored; lease end date and rent updated
and start the turnover routine. Ask why they are leaving and note it; patterns tell you about pricing and maintenance.
Follow local rules on notice periods and caps. Keep increases predictable; a tenant who can plan is more likely to stay.
Beatrix's lease ends this week and her renewal was offered at 1,960 dollars. She has not replied. The manager calls today; if she stays, the signed renewal goes in before the end date.

When a tenant pays on time and looks after the unit, say so. A short thank-you with the renewal offer, a fair increase and a small upgrade such as a new faucet or fresh paint costs far less than a vacant month, cleaning, and the risk of a worse tenant next.
No lease ends in the next 30 days without a decision
Every renewal offer has a reply-by date
Put the 90-day and 60-day dates for every lease on the team calendar the day the lease is signed, so no renewal starts late.
